Drinking Zamzam, and the talbiyah said often and aloud
Sunnah
Nothing, though the Hanafis and Malikis attach weight to the talbiyah at the entry into ihram.

sections.gloss: ahkam an-nisa, the rulings concerning women
sections.title: For women, and for the men travelling with them
sections.lead: Most of the fear a woman carries into this journey is about one thing, and it has a clear answer given by the Prophet ﷺ to Aisha while she was crying. The rest of this section is dress, hair, travel, and the honest state of a question the schools have never agreed on.

cards.t: Menstruation does not stop the Hajj
ps: Aisha entered ihram for Umrah and began menstruating before reaching Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ came in and found her weeping. He said: this is a thing Allah has decreed upon the daughters of Adam. Do what the pilgrim does, except do not perform tawaf around the House until you become pure.

Read the exception carefully, because everything hangs on it. She does what the pilgrim does. She enters ihram, she says the talbiyah, she stands at Arafah, she stays at Muzdalifah, she stones the pillars, her sacrifice is made, she cuts her hair, she is in the Hajj entirely. One act is paused: tawaf. And with it, since sa’i follows a valid tawaf, the sa’i waits too.

So a woman who begins to bleed on the seventh of Dhul Hijjah loses nothing of the Hajj. She performs tawaf al-ifadah when she becomes pure, even if that is on the twelfth or later, and she is excused the farewell tawaf entirely.
She should still make ghusl at the miqat, as Asma bint Umays was told to do after giving birth at Dhul Hulayfah. The washing is for the state of ihram, not for purity from bleeding.

refs.note: do what the pilgrim does, except do not perform tawaf until you are pure
in the book of Hajj, Aisha’s longer account of the Farewell Hajj: do what the pilgrim does, except do not circle the House until you are pure
the menstruating woman leaves without the farewell tawaf

cards.t: The hard case: the flight leaves and she is not pure
ps: Tawaf al-ifadah is a pillar. It cannot be skipped, it cannot be bought off, and until it is performed she is still in ihram, which means her husband remains unlawful to her. And modern travel puts a fixed departure date on a body that keeps its own calendar. This is the genuinely difficult problem of this section, and it deserves an honest answer rather than a comfortable one.
The classical majority is firm: purity is a condition of tawaf, so she waits, even if it costs her the flight. Groups have historically kept a woman behind with a mahram until she became pure.

A second position, argued by Ibn Taymiyyah and adopted by a number of contemporary scholars and fatwa councils for cases of real necessity, holds that a woman in this position may perform tawaf al-ifadah while menstruating, taking precautions, because the requirement of purity for tawaf is not established by an explicit text of the same strength as the obligation itself, and because the alternative places on her a hardship the law does not impose. Some who permit it require a sacrifice with it and some do not.
Do not decide this from a page. Decide it with a scholar who can hear the actual circumstances. But go knowing that the question has an answer and that scholars have thought about you.
schools: Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali
purity is a condition of tawaf; she waits until she is pure, whatever it costs in travel.
Hanafi
the tawaf is valid though sinful, and a badanah, a camel, is due for performing it in a state of major impurity, and repeating it while pure is better.
Ibn Taymiyyah and a number of contemporary councils
permit it in genuine necessity, with precautions, for a woman who cannot remain and cannot return.

refs.note: tawaf around the House is a prayer, except that Allah has permitted speech in it; the report the majority lean on here, which is not in the two Sahihs, whose raising to the Prophet is discussed, and which a number of scholars treat as the statement of Ibn Abbas
He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship

cards.t: Dress, hair, and prayer
ps: There is no special ihram garment for a woman. She wears her ordinary modest clothing, in any colour she likes, and there is no requirement of white. What is prohibited to her specifically is the niqab, a veil cut and fitted to the face, and gloves, because those two were named. Her face and hands are otherwise uncovered in ihram, which is the point of naming them.

She may still lower a loose cloth from her head over her face when men are passing, which is what Aisha described the women doing on the journey. The schools differ over whether that cloth may rest against the face: the Hanafis hold it should be kept off it, by a stiffened edge or a cap, and others permit contact.
For the hair, taqsir only. She takes about a fingertip’s length from the ends, gathering the hair or taking from each braid. Women do not shave.

She may not pray or fast while menstruating, and she does not make up the prayers. She may make du’a, say dhikr, say the talbiyah, recite from memory according to many scholars, carry her supplication list, and stand at Arafah for the whole afternoon with her hands raised. None of that is closed to her, and Arafah is not a prayer.

refs.note: the narration of Ibn Umar: a woman in ihram does not wear the niqab nor the gloves
in the book of the rites, the narration of Aisha: the riders would pass us while we were in ihram with him ﷺ, and we would lower a cloth over the face
Ibn Abbas: women do not shave, women only shorten

cards.t: Travelling with a mahram
ps: A mahram is a man a woman can never marry: her father, son, brother, uncle, grandfather, father in law, and her husband is counted with them. The Prophet ﷺ said a woman should not travel except with a mahram, and in one narration a man said his wife had set out for Hajj and he was enlisted for an expedition, and he was told to go and perform Hajj with his wife.
Whether that makes a mahram a condition of the obligation of Hajj on a woman is one of the genuinely old disagreements, and both sides argue from evidence.

Two honest additions. First, the rules on the ground have changed: for several years now the authorities have permitted women to register for Hajj in a group of women without a mahram, which is a visa rule and not a fatwa, and it does not settle the fiqh question either way. Second, both sides of this disagreement are asking the same thing underneath: is she safe. Answer that question first, honestly, and then ask which school you are following.
schools: Hanafi and Hanbali
a mahram or husband is a condition of the obligation; without one, Hajj is not obligatory upon her, and travelling without one is not permitted.
Maliki and Shafi’i
for the obligatory Hajj she may travel with a trustworthy group; the Shafi’is speak of a group of trustworthy women and some of them permit less where safety is certain.
Both sides cite
Umar sending Uthman and Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf with the Prophet’s ﷺ wives on Hajj, and the report of a woman travelling from Hirah to the House fearing none but Allah.

refs.note: the narration of Ibn Abbas: a woman does not travel except with a mahram, and the man told to go and perform Hajj with his wife
the narration that Umar permitted the wives of the Prophet ﷺ their last Hajj and sent Uthman ibn Affan and Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf with them
the narration of Adi ibn Hatim: a woman will travel from Hirah to circle the House fearing none but Allah

cards.t: Practical things nobody tells her
ps: Medication to delay a period is permitted by the great majority of contemporary scholars if a doctor says it is safe for her, and many women use it for exactly this journey. Start it well before travelling, not the week you fly, and expect it to be unreliable if you begin late.

In tawaf, stay in the outer rings. The reward is not in the metre. Umm Salamah performed tawaf riding, behind the people, on the Prophet’s ﷺ instruction, because she was unwell. There is nothing pious about being crushed.

Pack for the reality: unscented wipes, extra underwear, painkillers you already know you tolerate, a long light overhead garment that covers without heat, and shoes you have already walked twenty kilometres in.
And take this: your Hajj is not lesser. There is not a men’s Hajj and a women’s Hajj. The same standing, the same day, the same forgiveness, on a plain where nobody can tell who anyone is.

refs.note: in the book of Hajj, the narration of Umm Salamah, who complained of illness and was told to perform tawaf riding, behind the people

sections.gloss: al-jubran, the repairing of what was broken
sections.title: When something goes wrong
sections.lead: It will. Buses fail, crowds turn people back, bodies give out, and somebody wears scented soap on the ninth. The law has a whole chapter for this, and its temper is merciful. Most of what goes wrong costs a sheep. A little costs nothing. One thing cannot be repaired at all, and even that has a way out.

cards.t: The short version, before the detail
ps: Leaving an obligation costs a dam, a sacrifice: a sheep or a goat, or a seventh share of a camel or a cow, slaughtered inside the sanctuary and given to its poor. Your group can arrange it, and in Makkah so can any of the licensed offices.
Breaking a prohibition of ihram costs a fidyah: fasting three days, or feeding six poor people, or slaughtering a sheep, your choice of the three.
Sins of speech and temper cost repentance, and an apology to the person.
Missing the standing at Arafah cannot be repaired, and it is the only one.

And the instruction that outranks this whole page: ask a scholar on site. Every group has one. The Haram has fatwa desks. Do not guess, do not act on what the man in the next bunk told you, and do not let embarrassment stop you, because the people answering these questions have heard everything, every year, for their whole lives.

refs.note: the threefold expiation of fasting, charity, or sacrifice
ask the people of knowledge if you do not know

cards.t: Missing Arafah
ps: If dawn on the tenth arrives and you were not at Arafah at any point in the window, the Hajj is missed. The scholars call this fawat al-Hajj, and they set out what happens next rather than leaving a person stranded.

You come out of ihram by performing the acts of an Umrah: tawaf, sa’i, and cutting the hair. A sacrifice is due. And you make up the Hajj the following year. That is the position of the four schools, taken from the rulings of Umar and other companions on people this happened to.

It is worth knowing why the schools require the make up even when the Hajj was voluntary: the Qur’an commands the completion of the Hajj and the Umrah once entered, so entering voluntarily makes finishing binding.
schools: The four schools
the missed Hajj is exited with the acts of an Umrah, a sacrifice is due, and the Hajj is made up the following year.
A minority of scholars
hold no make up is due for one who had only intended a voluntary Hajj; this is not the position of the four schools.

refs.note: and complete the Hajj and the Umrah for Allah
whoever caught the standing before dawn of the tenth has caught the Hajj

cards.t: Being prevented from finishing
ps: If you are physically stopped from completing the rites, by a closed border, an illness that makes movement impossible, an arrest, an accident, the Qur’an addresses you directly: if you are prevented, then whatever sacrifice is easy. You slaughter where you are held, cut your hair, and come out of ihram.

There is a sunnah worth using before you ever leave home. Duba’ah bint az-Zubayr was ill and afraid she could not complete the journey. The Prophet ﷺ told her to perform Hajj and to stipulate a condition: O Allah, my place of release is wherever You hold me back. Whoever makes that condition at the moment of entering ihram, and is then genuinely prevented, comes out of ihram with no sacrifice due at all.

If you are elderly, unwell, or travelling with a condition that could stop you, say those words when you enter ihram. It costs nothing and it can save you a great deal. The Shafi’is and Hanbalis act on it fully; the Hanafis and Malikis do not give the condition the same effect.
schools: Shafi’i and Hanbali
the stipulation is valid and effective; the one prevented comes out of ihram with nothing due.
Hanafi and Maliki
the stipulation does not remove the consequences; the rules of being prevented apply as they otherwise would.

refs.note: if you are prevented, then whatever sacrifice is easy
the hadith of Duba’ah bint az-Zubayr: my place of release is wherever You hold me back

cards.t: Broke a prohibition without knowing
ps: The commonest version of this: you used the hotel’s scented soap, or a scented deodorant, or put on a shirt half asleep on a bus at four in the morning. The moment you realise, stop. Wash it off, take it off. Do not carry on because you have already ruined it, because you have not.
Whether an expiation is then due depends on the school, and this is one of the differences most worth carrying with you, because it decides whether you owe anything at all.

Under all four, a prohibition broken out of genuine need, an injury requiring a bandage, an illness requiring the head to be shaved, is permitted and carries the expiation without any sin, exactly as the Qur’an says of the one with an ailment of the head.
schools: Shafi’i and Hanbali
no expiation on the one who forgot or did not know, in perfume, clothing and covering the head, provided he stops at once.
Hanafi and Maliki

the standard summary is that the expiation is due even from the forgetful, because it repairs the rite rather than punishing the person, and the Hanafis reduce it to charity in a number of small cases. The summary flattens the Maliki position, which has recognised exceptions of its own, so ask before you assume you owe anything.
All four
hold that a prohibition done out of necessity is permitted and carries the expiation without sin.

refs.note: whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head, then a ransom of fasting, charity or sacrifice
the narration of Ka’b ibn Ujrah, whose head troubled him with lice, given the three choices of fasting, feeding or a sacrifice

cards.t: Lost count, missed a throw, could not get there
ps: Lost count in tawaf or sa’i: build on the smaller number you are certain of, and complete. Uncertainty in worship is settled by certainty, the way it is in prayer.

Missed a whole day’s stoning: most scholars have you make it up on the following day, throwing the missed day’s pebbles first and then that day’s, in order. Missing all of it until the days are over costs a sacrifice. Missing one or two pebbles is treated more lightly and the schools differ on the amount of charity due.

Could not reach the pillars at all through illness, disability, pregnancy or crowd danger: appoint someone. He throws his own seven first, then yours, at each pillar. This is agreed and it is not a lesser Hajj.

Left Mina early, or missed a night: this is where the difference between the schools actually saves people, since the Hanafis do not attach a sacrifice to the nights at Mina at all. Ask your group’s scholar which view they act on before you pay for a sheep you may not owe.

refs.note: the narration of Abu Sa’id al-Khudri: when one of you is uncertain, let him build on what he is certain of; stated of prayer and extended by the scholars
in the book of Hajj, the narration of Ibn Abbas: do it, and there is no harm, said to every question of order that day at Mina

cards.t: The mistakes that cost nothing
ps: Crying. Losing your temper and regretting it. Being unable to finish a du’a. Falling asleep at Arafah. Forgetting the words on Safa. Feeling nothing at all when you first see the Kaaba, while the person next to you weeps.

None of these are in any book of expiations, because none of them are defects. The Hajj is made of acts, and the acts were performed. What you felt while performing them is between you and Allah and is not always available on demand.
The sins of the tongue are different: they cost repentance, and where a person was hurt, they cost an apology. The Qur’an names them right at the start of the season for a reason.

refs.note: no obscenity, no corruption, no arguing in the Hajj
Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity

sections.title: Common mistakes, said gently
sections.lead: None of these are written to embarrass anyone. Every one of them is done by sincere people who were never taught otherwise, and most of them come from loving the place too much rather than too little. Knowing them beforehand is the only cure, because nobody has time to explain in a crowd.

cards.t: Fighting to reach the Black Stone
ps: Kissing al-Hajar al-Aswad is a sunnah. Elbowing a seventy year old woman out of the way to do it is a sin. A sunnah does not sit on top of a wrong, and no scholar in any school has ever said otherwise.

Umar walked up to the Stone and said: I know that you are a stone, you neither harm nor benefit, and were it not that I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ kissing you, I would not kiss you. It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ told Umar, who was strong, not to crowd at the Stone because he would harm the weak, and to face it and say the takbir if he could not reach it.

So: if there is space, kiss it. If not, raise your hand toward it, say Allahu akbar, and keep walking. You have done the sunnah. The version of this journey where you touch every stone and hurt three people is worth less than the version where you touch none.

refs.note: Umar: I know you are a stone that neither harms nor benefits
the report of Umar being told not to crowd at the Stone and to harm no one

cards.t: Believing every circuit has its own du’a
ps: Books are sold at every gate with a different supplication printed for each circuit of tawaf, and for each stretch of the sa’i. Nothing of the sort is established from the Prophet ﷺ. The only fixed words inside tawaf are the takbir at the Stone and the verse said between the Yamani corner and the Black Stone.

Two things go wrong when a person reads from a card. He spends the tawaf watching the page instead of asking for anything he wants, and he is thrown into a panic when he loses his place. Say what is in you. In your own language. That is not a lesser tawaf, it is the tawaf.
There is no harm in someone reciting a printed du’a because it helps him. The mistake is believing it is required, and correcting others who do not have one.

refs.note: the one fixed supplication in tawaf, between the two corners
in the book of the rites, the narration of Abdullah ibn as-Sa’ib: he ﷺ said the verse between the Yamani corner and the Black Stone

cards.t: Wiping the cloth, the walls, the Maqam
ps: The kiswah, the black cloth over the Kaaba, is replaced every year. Wiping it over your face, rubbing your children against it, tying threads to it or pressing your body against the walls and the corners for blessing has no basis in what the Prophet ﷺ or his companions did. Nor does touching the Maqam of Ibrahim, or the Yamani corner with the lips, or the other two corners at all.

Two things only were touched in the House: the Black Stone, kissed or touched, and the Yamani corner, touched with the hand. His companions were precise about this because they understood that in worship, adding is not loving more.

Standing at the multazam, the space between the Stone and the door, and making du’a there is reported of Ibn Abbas and some of the early generations, and a number of scholars permit it. It is also a place where people are routinely crushed. Know that it is a matter with some room in it, and that no one is required to reach it.

refs.note: in the book of Hajj, the narration of Ibn Umar: he ﷺ touched only the two Yamani corners
in the book of Hajj, the narration of Umar kissing the Black Stone, with the touching of the two Yamani corners described

cards.t: Thinking the pebbles hit devils
ps: People throw with rage. They shout. They throw shoes, umbrellas, water bottles, whole sandals, and every year someone throws a large stone that opens a stranger’s head, because they have been told they are stoning devils and they mean it.

There is no devil standing at the pillars. The pillars mark places, and the throwing is an act of obedience and remembrance. A report from Aisha states that the circling of the House, the going between Safa and Marwah, and the throwing of the pebbles were only established for the remembrance of Allah. Scholars have graded that report differently, and it is honest to say so, and its meaning is what every school teaches about these rites.

Throw seven small pebbles, the size of a chickpea, one at a time, saying Allahu akbar with each. The Prophet ﷺ held up such pebbles and said: with the like of these, throw. And in the same breath he warned against exaggeration in religion, and said that exaggeration is what destroyed the peoples before us. He said that at the Jamarat, on that morning, holding stones the size of beans.

refs.note: in the chapters on the rites, the narration of Ibn Abbas: with the like of these throw, and beware of exaggeration in religion
in the book of the rites, the report of Aisha that the circling of the House, the going between Safa and Marwah and the stoning were established for the remembrance of Allah; graded variously

cards.t: Arriving at Arafah with nothing left
ps: The commonest way to waste a Hajj is to spend everything before the ninth. Repeated Umrahs from at-Tan’im every other day. Night prayer until Fajr for a week. Shopping until midnight. Walking twenty kilometres a day in the sun in early Dhul Hijjah. Then Arafah arrives and the person sleeps through the afternoon of his life, or sits with a migraine unable to form a sentence.

Treat the days before as training and rest, not as the event. Drink water constantly, sleep in the afternoons, take your prayers in your room when the mosque is a forty minute walk in forty five degree heat, and let the extra Umrahs go. There is no established sunnah of repeating Umrah again and again in one journey; Aisha’s Umrah from at-Tan’im was a consolation for one that her period had interrupted.
Arrive at Arafah with something left. That is the whole strategy of the Hajj.

refs.note: in the book of Umrah, the narration of Aisha, sent out to at-Tan’im for the Umrah she had been unable to complete
in the book of faith, the narration of Abu Hurayrah: the religion is ease, and none makes it hard but it overcomes him, so take on only what you can sustain

cards.t: Guarding the rites and losing the people
ps: A man can be meticulous about ramal in the first three circuits and shove a stranger out of a queue for water an hour later. Everyone has seen it. Some of us have been it.

The Hajj is a rare place where every single interaction is with someone tired, hot, frightened, far from home and speaking another language. Feeding people, giving up a place, carrying a bag, being gentle in speech: when the Prophet ﷺ was asked what makes a Hajj accepted, the answer reported from him is feeding others and speaking well.

And know the boundary of what the journey erases. The Hajj wipes what is between a person and his Lord. It does not wipe what is owed to people: money you took, a reputation you damaged, a family member you cut off. The bankrupt of this ummah, he ﷺ said, is the one who comes with prayers and fasting and charity, and also with having insulted this one and struck that one, and his good deeds are handed over until they run out.
Settle it before you go, if you can. And if you cannot, go, and settle it when you return.

sections.gloss: az-zad, the provision for a journey
sections.title: Before you go
sections.lead: A packing list is not a spiritual document, but an unprepared body cannot stand at Arafah for six hours and an unsettled life cannot be left behind. Tick these off over the months before you travel. Nothing here is counted against you, and the list is kept in this browser only.

items: Passport valid well past your return date, and the visa and Hajj permit arranged through a licensed operator, not an intermediary who cannot be named.
Your operator’s full itinerary in writing: which camp at Mina, which tent number, which transport scheme, whether Muzdalifah is a full night or a shortened one.
Copies of every document in a second bag and a photograph of each on your phone.
Travel insurance, and the emergency number of your group leader saved and written on paper too.
The meningococcal vaccination, which is required, and any others your health authority names that year; requirements change annually, so check the current list rather than an old blog.
Walking fitness built over months: work up to ten to fifteen kilometres a day, in the shoes you will actually wear, including some walking in heat.
A doctor’s appointment if you have a chronic condition, and a letter listing your diagnoses and medicines in English.
Enough of every prescription medicine for the whole trip plus two weeks, in original packaging, split across two bags.
For women, a conversation with a doctor about whether to delay a period, started early enough to be reliable.
Two sets of ihram cloths for a man and a wide belt with a zip pocket, or for a woman two or three loose modest outfits in light fabric with long sleeves.
Unscented soap, unscented shampoo, unscented toothpaste and unscented deodorant, bought and packed deliberately.
Sandals that leave the top of the foot and the ankle open, already worn in, plus a cheap spare pair.
A light prayer mat, a small backpack, a refillable water bottle, an umbrella for the sun, a spray fan.
Oral rehydration sachets, painkillers, blister plasters, antiseptic cream, a thermometer, and anything you personally always need.
A drawstring bag for your shoes in the mosque, and a bright ribbon or tag so your group can spot you.
A small paper notebook: batteries die and networks fail, and you will want your du’a list at Arafah.
The talbiyah memorised, so you are not reading it at the miqat.
The words said on Safa and Marwah memorised, and the verse said between the two corners.
A written list of every person who asked you to make du’a for them, with names.
Your own list: the five things you have never asked anyone for. Write them before you fly.
Read this page again on the plane, and once more the night of the eighth.
Debts settled, or a written schedule agreed with whoever you owe.

A will written and witnessed, with someone trustworthy told where it is; the Prophet ﷺ said it is not right for a Muslim who has something to bequeath to pass two nights without his will written with him.
Forgiveness asked, by message or by call, of everyone you can think of who has a right against you, named specifically rather than in a general announcement.
Your family provided for while you are away, in money and in arrangements.
Any trust or deposit you are holding for someone returned or handed to someone reliable.

cards.t: Provision, and the best of it
ps: The Qur’an gives the packing instruction in the middle of the Hajj verses, and the whole sentence is worth memorising: take provision, and indeed the best provision is taqwa, being mindful of Allah. Commentators say it was revealed about people who set out for Hajj with no food, calling themselves reliant on Allah, and then begged from the pilgrims.
So the two halves belong together. Pack properly, because arriving as a burden on other people is not piety. And know that the sandals and the sachets are not what you are actually carrying there.

sections.title: What the journey is actually for
sections.lead: One short section, and then the room ends. Everything above is the how. This is the why, and it is the part that has to survive the flight home.

cards.t: Two pieces of white cloth
ps: A man in ihram is dressed in two unstitched white sheets. He will be dressed in something very similar once more, and he will not be putting it on himself.

That is not a morbid thought, it is the design. In the two cloths there is no way to tell a surgeon from a driver, a citizen of one country from a refugee of another, a man with three properties from a man with three shirts. Every marker a person spends his life assembling is taken off at a line in the desert. What is left standing on the plain at Arafah is the thing that will be raised, which is all any of us ever were.

People say the Hajj is a rehearsal for the Day of Standing. It is more exact than that. It is the same posture, the same clothing, the same crowd, the same helplessness, the same asking. The difference is that this time you chose to come, and you can still ask.

refs.note: you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time

cards.t: Returning as the day his mother bore him
ps: Whoever performs Hajj for Allah and does not speak obscenely nor act corruptly returns as the day his mother bore him. Sit with that sentence. Not forgiven a little. Not improved. Returned to the state of a newborn, who has never done anything at all.

A newborn has no history. That is the gift, and it is also the difficulty: a person returns with a clean page and immediately has to decide what to write on it. The scholars said the sign of an accepted Hajj is not what you felt at Arafah but what changed afterwards, and they said it because they had watched people come back unchanged.
So the last question of this room is a plain one. If Allah has just given you a page with nothing on it, what is the first thing you intend to put there.

refs.note: returns as the day his mother bore him
the accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise

cards.t: And then the ordinary life
ps: The Qur’an ends the Hajj passage by telling the pilgrims to remember Allah the way they used to remember their forefathers, or more intensely, and then it divides people by what they ask for: some say our Lord, give us in this world, and they have no share in the hereafter; and others say our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.

Then, immediately, the very next verses turn to ordinary life: the days of Tashriq, the person whose speech about worldly life impresses you while his heart is at war, the one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah. The Book moves from the plain of Arafah back to the street without pausing, because that was always where this was going.

You will land at an airport. Someone will be late to collect you. Within a week there will be a queue, a bill, a rude message. That week is the Hajj too. It is where the standing gets spent, or does not.

refs.note: remember Allah as you remember your forefathers, or more intensely
our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the hereafter
and remember Allah during the numbered days
it is not their meat nor their blood that reaches Allah, but your piety
